title: Posing Problems with Paper-Folding
author: Paul Rowlandson
summary: Paul Rowlandson shares a paper-folding activity, learned from a PGCE tutor, that he has used as an annual icebreaker with new classes: folding an A4 sheet into a tetrahedron through a sequence of folds. He argues the activity's real value is its versatility across the whole secondary maths curriculum, and spends the bulk of the post cataloguing questions teachers can pose at each stage. For KS2-3, he covers identifying and verifying shape properties (checking whether a folded triangle is really equilateral using congruence, symmetry, or angle-checking) and expressing areas of resulting shapes as fractions, percentages, or ratios of one another. For KS4, he shows how the same folds demonstrate that similar shapes with length ratio 1:n have area ratio 1:n-squared, and walks through a full trigonometric proof of why the folds produce a 60-degree angle. Rowlandson positions the post as a resource bank teachers can return to at multiple points across a student's maths education, not a single-use starter activity.
points: The activity's core pedagogical value is reusability across year groups -- the same physical folds support KS2-3 questions about shape properties and KS4 questions about similarity, scale factors, and formal proof.

Rowlandson's approach to 'proving' a folded triangle is equilateral (rather than just eyeballing it) models several distinct verification strategies -- folding to check congruent sides, checking rotational symmetry, and overlaying congruent triangles -- for the same underlying claim.
His scale-factor demonstration (lengths in ratio 1:2 produce areas in ratio 1:4, not 1:2) directly targets a well-known student misconception that area scale factor doubles rather than squares.
The KS4 trigonometric proof of the 60-degree fold angle shows how a hands-on activity can scaffold into a genuine formal-proof exercise rather than remaining purely manipulative.
quotes: What I particularly like about many paper-folding activities is their versatility to support or challenge pupils at different stages of their maths education.

We could ask pupils how they might check that they have identified certain shapes correctly. For example, after the first three folds, we have a triangle that looks equilateral. How could we check that it is equilateral?
My favourite use for this paper-folding task is to demonstrate that for two similar shapes with lengths in the ratio 1:n, their areas are in the ratio 1:n2.
I never feel that noticing squaring is obvious when using 2’s. Pupils might think that the area scale factor is double the length scale factor instead.

Quibbling about whether an angle at the corner of some paper is 1° out might seem a little trivial to some pupils. So, a slightly less pernickety approach could be to ask, "Why do these folds create an equilateral triangle?
Using exact trig values for sine, we can reason that the marked angle is 30°.
